count: {count} realm(s). Everything under a realm's prefix is that realm; everything under no prefix is the default one.
switchedOff: Trust realms are switched off. realms.enabled is false, so every prefix below answers 404 and this whole service is the default realm. The definitions are untouched — that is what this setting is for: it lets a realm be ruled out as the cause of something without anything being deleted. Turn it back on in the settings at the foot of this page.
switchedOnNone: Trust realms are switched ON and none has been defined, which is this service's ordinary state rather than something to fix. realms.enabled is true; the feature does nothing until a realm exists, because the built-in default realm has an empty prefix and IS this service. That is a property rather than a coincidence — a service with no realm defined behaves exactly as it did before realms existed, which is what keeps every client, container and test that predates them working unchanged. Define one below and its prefix starts answering immediately: a switcher appears on every page of this console, and GET /realms starts reporting active: true.
name: Name
idRuleHead: The id becomes a path segment, so it is lower-case letters, digits and hyphens. It may not be default and it may not be the first segment of a path this service already serves —
idRuleTail: — whatever realms.pathSegment is set to, precisely so that clearing that setting cannot turn an existing realm into a shadow over the console or the authorization server.
domainNote: The domain — iyasec.io, dev.iyasec.io — is the root of every NAME the realm invents: its directory is a tree of its own at the RFC 2247 mapping of it (iyasec.io is dc=iyasec,dc=io), its Kerberos realm is the domain in capitals, its SPIFFE trust domain is the domain, and its identity providers call themselves urn:<domain>:idp. It is not where the realm is REACHED — the issuer and every URL still come from the host a request arrived on. No two realms may share one; one inside another's is allowed and is a separate tree. It is fixed once the realm is created. Left empty it is <id>.{defaultDomain}.
separatedHeading: What is separated, and what is shared
separatedLead: A realm separates what this service ISSUES and everything it is holding while it issues it — keys, sessions, codes, tokens, offers, artifacts, statistics and the audit log — and since each realm has a directory of its own, the people, groups, applications and policies in it. The families on sockets with no path in them are told apart some other way, and a few things belong to the process and are shared. This table is the whole list, and GET /realms answers the same thing to a client that cannot read a console.
retiringHead: The realm {id} {state, select, interrupted {was being removed, and the removal was interrupted} other {is being removed}}.
finishElsewhere: You are reading this console inside it, so do it from another realm: the switcher at the top of the sidebar.
separatedBy: {how, select, path {by path} dn {by DN} name {by name} socket {by socket} other {by {how}}}
caveatIssues: A realm separates what this service ISSUES, not who it knows. Each realm has its own signing key, so a token minted in one does not verify against another's JWKS — that is the point of a realm rather than a side effect. Each realm also has a directory of its own — its own ou=users, ou=groups and ou=applications under dc=<id> — and so administrators of its own: the two role groups in that directory administer that realm and nothing outside it, while the default realm's two groups administer every realm. A new realm is seeded with an admin account that holds both. The table at the foot of this page is the whole list of what is separated how.
persistsBack: A realm defined here WILL come back. This process is running with persistence.mode={mode}, so the realm rows — their names, descriptions and per-realm settings — and each realm's own directory are written down and restored at the next start. WHAT DOES NOT COME BACK IS THE KEYS: every realm's signing key is regenerated on every start, exactly like the default realm's, so a token minted in this realm today verifies against nothing tomorrow. See
notPersistedHead: Nothing here is persisted on this process. Realms are held in memory and die with it, along with the keys they signed with. Define them from POST /admin-api/realms in whatever starts your stack if you want them back — or turn on
notPersistedTail: , which writes the realm registry and each realm's directory down. The KEYS are regenerated on every start either way.
nothingSet: Nothing. This realm is configured exactly as the process is — which is a realm that differs only in its key, its sessions and what it has issued.
readingInside: You are reading this console inside this realm. Every settings form in this console writes here.
readingInHead: You are reading this console in the
readingInTail: realm. The switcher on the left moves to this one; until then a settings form writes to the realm you are in, not to this one.
domainDetail: {domain}{builtin, select, yes {, from global.domain, fixed until a restart with another value} other {, fixed since the realm was created}}. Its directory is the tree at {baseDn}, a naming context of its own on the shared LDAP socket, and the names it invents — Kerberos realm, SPIFFE trust domain, entity IDs, the address a development-mode person is given — are built from it; the ones seeded when it was created are among its settings below.
prefixNote: Path prefix {prefix}. Every HTTP endpoint this service has is under it, unchanged: what is /oauth2/token in the default realm is {pathPrefix}/oauth2/token here.
kidNote: The signing key is {kid}, generated for this realm and held only in memory. A token minted here does not verify against any other realm's JWKS, which is what makes two realms two authorization servers rather than one served twice.
setsTail: can be set per realm, above whatever the process as a whole is configured with and below nothing. The two exceptions are realms.enabled and realms.pathSegment: a realm that could switch realms off, or move the prefix it was found under, would be doing it half way through the request that found it.
cannotRemove: Every URL this service published before trust realms existed is a URL in this realm, so removing it would remove the service. There is deliberately no button.
removeNote: Everything it holds goes with it — its sessions, its authorization codes, its tokens, its offers, its service providers, its statistics, its audit log and its signing key. That is deliberate rather than thorough: a realm re-created with the same id inheriting the last one's sessions would be the single most surprising thing a re-created realm could do. Nothing is removed from the shared directory, because nothing there belongs to a realm.
